title: Physics: Classical Mechanics & Thermodynamics
subtitle: Force, motion, energy & heat
methodology: METHODOLOGY · Every entry anchors to a landmark study, paper, clinical case or theoretical text. The hint explains the idea in plain language; the note names the primary publication and flags replication status, effect-size revisions and known controversies. Studies and effects carry a replicability badge — 🟢 robust · 🟡 nuanced or reduced · 🔴 failed or severely contested. Map pins mark the institution where the work was carried out.

categories.label: Theories & Models
categories.subtitle: The frameworks that organise force, motion, energy and heat

entries.label: Newton's Laws of Motion
entries.hint: Three deceptively simple rules — an object stays at rest or in constant motion unless a force acts on it; force equals mass times acceleration; every action has an equal and opposite reaction — turned out to be enough to derive essentially the whole of mechanics as it was understood for the next two centuries. The second law in particular, F=ma, became the single most-used equation in all of physics.
entries.note: Newton, I. (1687). Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica, Book I, Axioms or Laws of Motion. London: Royal Society, written while Newton was Lucasian Professor at Trinity College, Cambridge. Newton developed the underlying calculus needed to state and use these laws rigorously largely on his own, in parallel with (and in later bitter priority dispute with) Gottfried Leibniz.

entries.label: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
entries.hint: Every object with mass attracts every other object with mass, with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them — a single equation that, Newton showed, explains both an apple falling to the ground and the Moon's orbit around the Earth as the exact same phenomenon. It unified terrestrial and celestial physics, which had been treated as governed by entirely separate rules since antiquity.
entries.note: Newton, I. (1687). Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica, Book III, The System of the World. London: Royal Society. Newton reportedly first considered the inverse-square relationship in the 1660s but delayed publishing for two decades, partly to resolve whether a spherical mass could be treated as if all its mass were concentrated at its centre — a result requiring the calculus he was still developing.

entries.label: Conservation of Energy
entries.hint: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted between forms — kinetic, potential, thermal, chemical — with the total amount in any closed system always remaining exactly constant. Hermann von Helmholtz gave the first fully general statement of this principle across all of physics, building on more specific results, including Joule's experimental link between mechanical work and heat established a few years earlier.
entries.note: von Helmholtz, H. (1847). Über die Erhaltung der Kraft ['On the Conservation of Force']. Berlin: G. Reimer, presented to the Berlin Physical Society. Julius Robert von Mayer had proposed a similar principle independently in 1842, and James Prescott Joule was simultaneously establishing the mechanical equivalent of heat experimentally (see st2); priority disputes among the three ran for years, with Mayer in particular feeling overlooked, contributing to a nervous breakdown and suicide attempt in 1850.

entries.label: Simple Harmonic Motion
entries.hint: A pendulum, a mass on a spring, and countless other systems all obey the same underlying mathematical pattern when displaced slightly from equilibrium — a restoring force proportional to the displacement, producing smooth, repeating oscillation at a fixed frequency independent of amplitude. Christiaan Huygens gave this 'isochronism' its first rigorous mathematical treatment, directly enabling the pendulum clock's dramatically improved timekeeping accuracy.
entries.note: Huygens, C. (1673). Horologium Oscillatorium sive de Motu Pendulorum ['The Pendulum Clock']. Paris: F. Muguet, written while Huygens was based in The Hague and visiting Paris as a founding member of the French Academy of Sciences. Galileo had qualitatively observed pendulum isochronism decades earlier (reportedly timing a swinging cathedral lamp against his own pulse around 1602), but never developed the full mathematical theory Huygens provided.

entries.label: Bernoulli's Principle
entries.hint: Within a smoothly flowing fluid, speed and pressure trade off against each other — where the fluid moves faster, its pressure drops, and where it moves slower, pressure rises — a direct consequence of energy conservation applied to moving fluid. The principle explains how aircraft wings generate lift and why a shower curtain billows inward, from the exact same underlying relationship.
entries.note: Bernoulli, D. (1738). Hydrodynamica, sive de viribus et motibus fluidorum commentarii. Strasbourg: Johann Reinhold Dulsecker, written while Bernoulli held a professorship at the University of Basel. The principle strictly applies only to idealised, non-viscous ('inviscid') flow with no energy lost to friction — real fluids always deviate to some degree, a gap that later motivated the study of viscosity and, eventually, d'Alembert's paradox.

entries.label: The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
entries.hint: If system A is in thermal equilibrium with system B, and system B is in thermal equilibrium with system C, then A and C are automatically in thermal equilibrium with each other too — a seemingly obvious statement that turns out to be the logical foundation making temperature itself a well-defined, comparable quantity in the first place. It was recognised as necessary only after the First and Second Laws were already established, hence its unusual 'zeroth' numbering.
entries.note: Fowler, R.H. (1931), formalised in Fowler, R.H. & Guggenheim, E.A. (1939). Statistical Thermodynamics. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. The law had been implicitly assumed by every thermodynamicist since the concept of temperature was first quantified, but nobody had stated it as an explicit, independent axiom until Fowler pointed out that the First and Second Laws quietly presuppose it.

entries.label: The First Law of Thermodynamics
entries.hint: A system's internal energy changes exactly according to the heat added to it minus the work it does on its surroundings — energy conservation restated specifically for thermal systems, formally uniting the previously separate concepts of heat and mechanical work into a single unified bookkeeping principle. It closed the case, definitively, on the old 'caloric theory' idea that heat was a substance that simply flowed from hot to cold objects.
entries.note: Clausius, R. (1850). 'Über die bewegende Kraft der Wärme.' Annalen der Physik, 155(3), 368–397, written while Clausius taught at the Royal Artillery and Engineering School, Berlin. The paper simultaneously introduced what became the Second Law (see th8) in an early form, making 1850 something of a founding year for thermodynamics as a coherent, unified theory rather than two separate lines of inquiry about heat and mechanics.

entries.label: The Second Law of Thermodynamics & Entropy
entries.hint: Heat never spontaneously flows from a colder body to a hotter one, and in any real process, a quantity Clausius named 'entropy' can only stay the same or increase, never decrease, for the universe as a whole. The law explains why so many everyday processes — an ice cube melting, a dropped egg breaking — happen easily in one direction and essentially never reverse themselves, despite nothing in Newton's laws alone forbidding the reverse.
entries.note: Clausius, R. (1865). 'Über verschiedene für die Anwendung bequeme Formen der Hauptgleichungen der mechanischen Wärmetheorie.' Annalen der Physik, 125, 353–400, written while Clausius held a professorship at ETH Zurich. Clausius deliberately coined 'entropy' from the Greek for 'transformation,' choosing a word that sounded close to 'energy' since he considered the two concepts closely related; Boltzmann's later statistical reinterpretation (see st6) gave entropy its now-standard probabilistic meaning.

entries.label: Kinetic Theory of Gases
entries.hint: A gas's macroscopic properties — pressure, temperature, volume — can be derived entirely from treating it as vast numbers of tiny particles in ceaseless random motion, colliding elastically with each other and their container's walls. James Clerk Maxwell showed pressure itself is really just the statistical average of countless individual molecular impacts, reframing thermodynamics as, at bottom, a branch of statistics and mechanics rather than a separate science of heat.
entries.note: Maxwell, J.C. (1860). 'Illustrations of the Dynamical Theory of Gases.' Philosophical Magazine, 4th series, 19–20, written shortly after Maxwell's appointment at King's College London. Maxwell's original derivation contained a subtle statistical assumption he later recognised as unjustified, prompting a more rigorous follow-up paper in 1867 (see st5); the kinetic theory was independently and even more thoroughly developed by Ludwig Boltzmann over the following decade.

entries.label: Lagrangian Mechanics
entries.hint: Instead of tracking every force acting on every part of a system, Lagrangian mechanics reformulates the whole problem around a single scalar quantity — kinetic energy minus potential energy — and a principle that the system's actual path through time is exactly the one that makes this quantity's total accumulation stationary. The reformulation is often dramatically easier to work with for complex, constrained systems, and generalises far beyond the specific coordinate systems Newton's original formulation was tied to.
entries.note: Lagrange, J.L. (1788). Mécanique analytique. Paris: Veuve Desaint, completed shortly after Lagrange moved from the Berlin Academy to the Paris Académie des Sciences. Lagrange reportedly took considerable pride in the fact that the book contained not a single diagram, treating mechanics as a branch of pure analysis; the underlying calculus-of-variations machinery is covered from the mathematics side in the applied-math-statistics folio.

entries.label: Hamiltonian Mechanics
entries.hint: William Rowan Hamilton reformulated mechanics a second time, replacing Lagrange's velocity-based description with one built around momentum and position treated as independent, symmetric variables living in an abstract 'phase space.' The resulting equations turned out, a century later, to translate almost directly into the mathematical structure of quantum mechanics, making Hamilton's reformulation the specific bridge historically used to build quantum theory on top of classical foundations.
entries.note: Hamilton, W.R. (1833). 'On a General Method of Expressing the Paths of Light and of the Planets by the Coefficients of a Characteristic Function.' Dublin University Review, written at Dunsink Observatory, where Hamilton served as Royal Astronomer of Ireland from age 22. Hamilton originally developed the underlying mathematics to unify optics and mechanics, only later recognising its full generality for dynamics; the phase-space formulation is what modern chaos theory and statistical mechanics are built on top of.

categories.label: Landmark Studies
categories.subtitle: The defining experiments — and exactly what they found

entries.label: The Cavendish Experiment
entries.hint: Henry Cavendish measured the gravitational attraction between lead spheres in his own home, using an exquisitely sensitive torsion balance to detect a force so weak it had never been directly measured before — and from it calculated the first accurate value for the gravitational constant, and with it, the first accurate estimate of the Earth's mass and density. The experiment demonstrated Newton's law of gravitation applied at laboratory scale, not just to planets.
entries.note: Cavendish, H. (1798). 'Experiments to Determine the Density of the Earth.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 88, 469–526, conducted at Cavendish's home in Clapham, London, using an apparatus originally designed by geologist John Michell, who died before completing it himself. Cavendish's result for Earth's density was within about 1% of the modern accepted value, an extraordinary level of precision for eighteenth-century instrumentation.

entries.label: Joule's Mechanical Equivalent of Heat
entries.hint: James Prescott Joule used a falling weight to turn a paddle wheel inside an insulated water tank, precisely measuring how much the water's temperature rose for a given amount of mechanical work done — establishing, against considerable initial skepticism, that heat and mechanical energy are directly interconvertible at a fixed, measurable exchange rate. It was the crucial experimental evidence underneath the theoretical principle of energy conservation formalised a few years later.
entries.note: Joule, J.P. (1843–1850). A series of papers culminating in 'On the Mechanical Equivalent of Heat.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 140 (1850), 61–82, conducted largely in a private laboratory attached to Joule's family brewery in Manchester. Joule funded this research entirely himself, without a university position, and his early results were initially received with considerable skepticism by the physics establishment, including a famously cool reception at the 1847 British Association meeting.

entries.label: Carnot's Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire
entries.hint: Sadi Carnot, analysing the newly dominant steam engine, proved that any heat engine's efficiency is fundamentally capped by the temperature difference it operates across, no matter how cleverly it's engineered — an idealised maximum ('Carnot efficiency') that real engines can only approach, never exceed or equal. Written before the concept of energy conservation itself was established, it is now recognised as the founding text of thermodynamics as a discipline.
entries.note: Carnot, S. (1824). Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu. Paris: Bachelier. Carnot still worked within the outdated caloric theory of heat (that heat was a conserved fluid substance), yet his conclusions about maximum efficiency remain exactly correct under the modern theory — a striking case of a right answer surviving a wrong underlying model. Carnot died of cholera at 36 in 1832, and most of his papers were burned as a public health precaution, destroying further unpublished work.

entries.label: Clausius's Statement of the Second Law
entries.hint: Rudolf Clausius stated, in essentially the same paper that established the First Law, that heat cannot spontaneously pass from a colder to a hotter body without some other compensating change occurring elsewhere — a deceptively modest-sounding claim that turned out to impose a strict directionality on all physical processes, one Newton's mechanics alone never required.
entries.note: Clausius, R. (1850). 'Über die bewegende Kraft der Wärme.' Annalen der Physik, 155(3), 368–397. William Thomson (later Lord Kelvin) independently proposed an equivalent statement the same year, framed instead around the impossibility of converting heat entirely into work with no other effect; the two formulations were shown fully equivalent shortly afterward, and are still both taught as standard textbook statements of the Second Law today.

entries.label: Maxwell's Rigorous Velocity Distribution
entries.hint: Not every gas molecule moves at the same speed — Maxwell derived the precise statistical distribution of molecular speeds within a gas at a given temperature, a smooth bell-like curve now bearing his name, correcting a flawed statistical assumption in his own earlier 1860 derivation. It gave kinetic theory its first fully rigorous mathematical foundation, rather than a plausible but imprecisely justified sketch.
entries.note: Maxwell, J.C. (1867). 'On the Dynamical Theory of Gases.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 157, 49–88. Ludwig Boltzmann generalised the result further over the following decade, giving the now-standard 'Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution' its full form including the effect of external potential energy, not merely kinetic energy alone.

entries.label: Boltzmann's Statistical Entropy Formula
entries.hint: Ludwig Boltzmann showed that entropy, previously just a mysterious thermodynamic bookkeeping quantity, has a precise statistical meaning: it measures the number of distinct microscopic arrangements of a system's particles that all produce the same observable macroscopic state, with more probable (higher-entropy) states simply being the ones reachable by vastly more microscopic arrangements. The formula, S = k log W, is carved on Boltzmann's tombstone in Vienna.
entries.note: Boltzmann, L. (1877). 'Über die Beziehung zwischen dem zweiten Hauptsatze der mechanischen Wärmetheorie und der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung.' Wiener Berichte, 76, 373–435. The constant k, now called Boltzmann's constant, was actually named and first given its symbol by Max Planck decades later; Boltzmann's statistical approach was fiercely contested by contemporaries who doubted the physical reality of atoms (see db1), a dispute Boltzmann never lived to see fully resolved.

entries.label: Foucault's Pendulum
entries.hint: Léon Foucault suspended a heavy pendulum from the dome of the Panthéon in Paris and showed its swing plane slowly rotated over the course of a day, relative to the floor beneath it — direct, visible mechanical proof that the Earth itself was rotating, without needing to look at the sky at all. It was the first purely terrestrial, mechanical demonstration of Earth's rotation, over two centuries after Copernicus and Galileo had argued for it on astronomical grounds alone.
entries.note: Foucault, L. (1851). Public demonstration, Panthéon, Paris, following an initial private demonstration at the Paris Observatory weeks earlier. The pendulum's swing plane rotates at a rate depending on latitude — a full rotation takes about 32 hours in Paris, would take exactly 24 hours at the North or South Pole, and would not rotate at all on the equator — a direct, calculable consequence of the Coriolis effect (see ef9).

entries.label: Torricelli's Barometer
entries.hint: Evangelista Torricelli filled a long glass tube with mercury, inverted it into a mercury-filled dish, and found the mercury column settled at a consistent height, leaving a space above it — proving, against the prevailing Aristotelian belief that 'nature abhors a vacuum,' that this space was a genuine vacuum, and that ordinary atmospheric pressure alone was what held the mercury column up. It was the first deliberately created and scientifically studied vacuum in history.
entries.note: Torricelli, E. (1643). Described in a letter to Michelangelo Ricci, June 1644, conducted in Florence where Torricelli had succeeded Galileo as court mathematician to the Grand Duke of Tuscany. Blaise Pascal later had the experiment repeated at different altitudes on the Puy de Dôme mountain in 1648, confirming that the mercury column's height dropped with elevation exactly as predicted if atmospheric pressure, not some other force, was responsible.

entries.label: Perrin's Confirmation of Atomic Theory via Brownian Motion
entries.hint: Jean Perrin experimentally tracked the erratic, jittery motion of microscopic particles suspended in water, precisely measuring their statistical behaviour and confirming Einstein's 1905 theoretical prediction that this motion is caused by countless random collisions with individual water molecules. It was the decisive experimental evidence that finally convinced the small remaining group of skeptical physicists, including Wilhelm Ostwald, that atoms and molecules were genuinely real physical objects rather than a convenient calculating fiction.
entries.note: Perrin, J. (1909). 'Mouvement brownien et réalité moléculaire.' Annales de Chimie et de Physique, 18, 5–114, at the Sorbonne, Paris, directly testing Einstein, A. (1905). 'Über die von der molekularkinetischen Theorie der Wärme geforderte Bewegung von in ruhenden Flüssigkeiten suspendierten Teilchen.' Annalen der Physik, 17, 549–560. Perrin's measurements also gave one of the first accurate experimental determinations of Avogadro's number; he received the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics largely for this work.

entries.label: Poincaré's Discovery of Chaos in the Three-Body Problem
entries.hint: While competing for a prize offered by King Oscar II of Sweden for solving the general three-body gravitational problem, Henri Poincaré discovered something far stranger than a solution: the motion of even just three mutually gravitating bodies can become so sensitively dependent on their exact starting conditions that long-term prediction becomes effectively impossible, even though the underlying equations are completely deterministic. It was the first rigorous mathematical demonstration of what would later be called chaos.
entries.note: Poincaré, H. (1890). 'Sur le problème des trois corps et les équations de la dynamique.' Acta Mathematica, 13, 1–270 — a substantially revised version of Poincaré's original 1889 prize-winning memoir, after a serious error was discovered post-award requiring extensive (and expensive) reprinting. The full implications of Poincaré's discovery were not widely appreciated until Edward Lorenz's independent rediscovery of sensitive dependence in weather models seven decades later.

entries.label: Reynolds's Pipe Flow Experiments
entries.hint: Osborne Reynolds injected a thin stream of dye into water flowing through a glass pipe and found the flow abruptly transitioned from smooth, orderly layers to chaotic, swirling turbulence once the flow speed crossed a specific threshold — a transition depending not on speed alone but on a single dimensionless combination of speed, pipe size, and fluid viscosity, now called the Reynolds number. It gave engineers the first predictive, quantitative tool for anticipating when a given flow would turn turbulent.
entries.note: Reynolds, O. (1883). 'An Experimental Investigation of the Circumstances Which Determine Whether the Motion of Water Shall Be Direct or Sinuous.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 174, 935–982, at Owens College, Manchester. The Reynolds number remains the standard tool for predicting laminar-to-turbulent transition across scales from blood flow in capillaries to airflow over aircraft wings; a complete theoretical account of turbulence itself remains unsolved (see db8).

categories.label: Effects & Phenomena
categories.subtitle: Named, replicable patterns in mechanical and thermal systems

entries.label: Brownian Motion
entries.hint: Pollen grains suspended in water, viewed under a microscope, jitter and dart about in a continuous, erratic zigzag with no apparent cause — a botanist's curiosity for eight decades until it turned out to be direct visible evidence of individual water molecules colliding with each particle from random directions. It gave physicists their first genuine window onto molecular-scale motion, using nothing more than an ordinary light microscope.
entries.note: Brown, R. (1828). 'A Brief Account of Microscopical Observations...' Philosophical Magazine, 4(21), 161–173, based on observations made in London in 1827. Brown himself, a botanist, ruled out that the motion was biological (it persisted in mineral dust particles too) but offered no physical explanation; Einstein's 1905 theoretical treatment and Perrin's 1908 experimental confirmation (see st9) are what finally explained it as molecular bombardment.

entries.label: Resonance Disasters
entries.hint: A structure driven by a periodic force at or near its own natural oscillation frequency can build up dramatically larger swings than the driving force alone would suggest, even from a relatively gentle, steady input — as the Tacoma Narrows Bridge demonstrated spectacularly when moderate, steady winds excited a self-reinforcing twisting oscillation that tore the deck apart within months of the bridge opening.
entries.note: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed 7 November 1940, filmed extensively and widely used in physics education ever since. The popular explanation — simple wind-driven mechanical resonance — is now considered incomplete by structural engineers; the dominant modern account instead attributes the collapse to aeroelastic flutter, a self-sustaining feedback loop between the bridge's motion and the airflow around it, related to but more complex than textbook resonance alone.

entries.label: The Magnus Effect
entries.hint: A spinning object moving through a fluid curves away from a straight path, because its spin drags fluid around with it, speeding up flow on one side and slowing it on the other — producing a pressure difference, and with it a sideways force, entirely separate from ordinary lift or drag. It's why a well-struck soccer free kick curves around a defensive wall, and why golf balls are deliberately given backspin.
entries.note: Magnus, G. (1852). 'Über die Abweichung der Geschosse.' Abhandlungen der Königlichen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin, 1–23, originally investigating why spinning artillery shells veered off course. Isaac Newton had already qualitatively noted the same effect on tennis balls in a 1671 letter to the Royal Society, nearly two centuries earlier, without giving it a quantitative explanation.

entries.label: Terminal Velocity
entries.hint: An object falling through a fluid speeds up only until the fluid's drag force grows to exactly match gravity's pull, after which it falls at a constant 'terminal' speed no matter how much further it falls — which is why a raindrop and a skydiver both reach a stable falling speed rather than accelerating indefinitely. The specific terminal speed depends on the object's size, shape, and density, and the fluid's viscosity, in a precise mathematical relationship for small, slow-moving spheres.
entries.note: Stokes, G.G. (1851). 'On the Effect of the Internal Friction of Fluids on the Motion of Pendulums.' Transactions of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, 9, 8–106, giving the drag law (Stokes' Law) that predicts terminal velocity for small spheres in viscous flow at low Reynolds number. The law breaks down at higher speeds and larger sizes, exactly where Reynolds's later turbulence work (see st11) becomes the relevant description instead.

entries.label: Maxwell's Demon
entries.hint: Imagine a tiny, intelligent being guarding a trapdoor between two gas-filled chambers, letting only fast molecules pass one way and slow ones the other, sorting a uniform-temperature gas into a hot side and a cold side without doing any apparent work — seemingly violating the Second Law of Thermodynamics for free. The thought experiment exposed a genuine conceptual gap between thermodynamics and the underlying mechanics that took over a century to fully resolve.
entries.note: Maxwell, J.C. Letter to Peter Guthrie Tait, 11 December 1867, first published publicly in Maxwell's Theory of Heat (1871), London: Longmans, Green. Leó Szilárd (1929) and later Rolf Landauer (1961) and Charles Bennett (1982) showed the demon must expend energy specifically to erase its own memory of each molecule it has sorted, restoring consistency with the Second Law — the resolution ties thermodynamic entropy directly to information itself (see db2).

entries.label: The Mpemba Effect
entries.hint: Under some specific conditions, initially warmer water can freeze faster than initially cooler water placed in the same freezer — a claim that sounds like it should be impossible, since the warmer water has to pass through the cooler water's exact starting temperature on its way down. Erasto Mpemba, then a secondary school student, insisted on the effect against his own physics teacher's skepticism, and it was later confirmed experimentally, though a single agreed explanation for exactly which mechanism causes it remains unsettled.
entries.note: Mpemba, E.B. & Osborne, D.G. (1969). 'Cool?' Physics Education, 4(3), 172–175, University College, Dar es Salaam. Proposed explanations include enhanced evaporative cooling, convection currents, dissolved gas differences, and supercooling effects, and the effect's reproducibility itself has been disputed by some subsequent careful replications that found it highly sensitive to container shape and exact experimental protocol; a 2016 study argued much of the reported effect may be a measurement artifact.

entries.label: The Chaotic Tumbling of Saturn's Moon Hyperion
entries.hint: Most moons rotate in smooth, predictable lockstep with their orbit, always showing the same face to their planet — but Saturn's irregularly shaped moon Hyperion tumbles chaotically and unpredictably instead, its orientation impossible to forecast far in advance even with a perfectly precise model of the gravitational forces acting on it. It was the first celestial body confirmed to exhibit genuine chaotic rotation, extending Poincaré's abstract mathematical discovery to an object astronomers could actually observe.
entries.note: Wisdom, J., Peale, S.J. & Mignard, F. (1984). 'The Chaotic Rotation of Hyperion.' Icarus, 58(2), 137–152, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Voyager 2's 1981 flyby images, showing Hyperion's unusual sponge-like, irregular shape, motivated the theoretical prediction; subsequent Cassini mission observations (2005) confirmed the tumbling directly, exactly as the chaotic-dynamics model predicted.

entries.label: Gyroscopic Precession
entries.hint: A spinning top or wheel, pushed to tip over, doesn't simply fall in the direction it's pushed — instead its spin axis slowly sweeps out a cone, precessing sideways, in a direction at right angles to the push. The counterintuitive result follows directly from treating angular momentum as a vector quantity that a torque changes exactly the way force changes ordinary momentum, just rotated ninety degrees by the mathematics of rotational motion.
entries.note: Foucault, L. (1852) built and named the first laboratory gyroscope specifically to demonstrate the effect and further confirm Earth's rotation, extending his pendulum demonstration the previous year (see st7). The same physics keeps a spinning bicycle wheel or top upright, stabilises spinning artillery shells and rifle bullets in flight, and underlies the gyrocompass, used in ships and aircraft for over a century as a directional reference independent of magnetic fields.

entries.label: The Coriolis Effect
entries.hint: An object moving across a rotating surface appears, to an observer standing on that surface, to curve sideways — not because any real sideways force is acting on it, but because the surface itself is rotating out from underneath the object's actual straight-line path. It's why hurricanes rotate counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern, and why long-range artillery and missile guidance must explicitly correct for it.
entries.note: Coriolis, G.G. de (1835). 'Sur les équations du mouvement relatif des systèmes de corps.' Journal de l'École Polytechnique, 15, 142–154, originally derived for analysing rotating machinery like waterwheels, with no immediate reference to weather or the Earth. Its atmospheric and oceanic significance was only fully appreciated decades later, once large-scale weather observation made the characteristic rotational deflection of storm systems visible.

categories.label: Key Concepts
categories.subtitle: The building blocks and vocabulary every student must command

entries.label: Inertial Reference Frames
entries.hint: An inertial frame is any viewpoint moving at constant velocity — not accelerating or rotating — from which Newton's laws hold in their simplest form without needing extra fictitious forces to explain what's observed. Galileo's famous ship analogy, that no experiment performed below deck can tell you whether the ship is at rest or sailing smoothly, is the founding statement of the principle that physics itself looks identical in any such frame.
entries.note: Galileo, G. (1632). Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi del mondo ['Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems']. Florence, written largely while Galileo lived under house arrest at his villa in Arcetri. Newton's first law of motion (see th1) is essentially a formal restatement of this Galilean relativity principle; Einstein's special relativity (covered in the quantum-nuclear-relativity folio) generalises it further to include the constancy of the speed of light.

entries.label: Momentum & Impulse
entries.hint: Momentum — mass times velocity — is conserved in any collision between objects with no external forces acting, letting the outcome of a crash or impact be calculated without knowing any details of the complicated forces involved during the collision itself, only the situation immediately before and after. Impulse, a force applied over time, is exactly what's needed to change an object's momentum by a given amount.
entries.note: Wallis, J. (1670). Mechanica sive de Motu, Tractatus Geometricus. London, written while Wallis held the Savilian Chair of Geometry at Oxford. Wallis, Christopher Wren, and Christiaan Huygens independently submitted correct rules for collisions to the Royal Society within months of each other in 1668–69, prompted by a specific Society challenge; Newton's Principia (1687) later derived momentum conservation as a direct consequence of his third law.

entries.label: Center of Mass
entries.hint: Any rigid object, however irregularly shaped, behaves under gravity and in free motion as if its entire mass were concentrated at one specific point — its centre of mass — dramatically simplifying the analysis of complicated bodies down to the motion of a single equivalent point particle. A lever balances exactly at its centre of mass, and a thrown hammer's centre of mass traces the same smooth parabola a thrown ball would, however wildly the hammer itself tumbles.
entries.note: Archimedes. On the Equilibrium of Planes (c. 250 BCE), Syracuse, giving the first rigorous mathematical treatment of the centre of gravity for levers and simple shapes, building on earlier informal Greek work on the balance. Archimedes' approach used a form of proof by exhaustion related to methods that anticipated integral calculus by nearly two thousand years; most of his original manuscripts survive only through later Byzantine and Arabic copies.

entries.label: Potential Energy Landscapes
entries.hint: Potential energy is energy stored by an object's position or configuration — height in a gravitational field, compression in a spring — and plotting it as a landscape over all possible configurations turns finding a system's stable resting points into simply finding the landscape's valleys, and finding how a system evolves into simply asking which way is 'downhill' at any given point. The framework works identically whether the 'landscape' describes a literal hillside or an abstract configuration space with no direct physical geometry at all.
entries.note: Rankine, W.J.M. (1853). 'On the General Law of the Transformation of Energy.' Proceedings of the Philosophical Society of Glasgow, 3, 276–280, at the University of Glasgow — the paper that coined the term 'potential energy' itself, generalising William Thomson's and others' earlier, more specific treatments of stored mechanical energy. The landscape picture extends directly into chemistry (reaction energy landscapes) and into the phase-space formulations of analytical mechanics (see th11).

entries.label: Phase Space & Liouville's Theorem
entries.hint: Phase space represents a system's complete state — every position and every momentum of every particle — as a single point in a high-dimensional abstract space, so that the system's entire time evolution becomes one continuous trajectory through that space. Joseph Liouville proved that as a group of nearby starting points evolves forward in time, the volume they collectively occupy in phase space never changes, even as its shape stretches and distorts — a conservation law with no obvious counterpart in ordinary physical space.
entries.note: Liouville, J. (1838). 'Note sur la théorie de la variation des constantes arbitraires.' Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées, 3, 342–349, at the Sorbonne, Paris. Liouville's theorem became essential to statistical mechanics, since it guarantees that a probability distribution spread across phase space behaves like an incompressible fluid, a property Gibbs's later ensemble formulation (see co9) depends on directly.

entries.label: Equilibrium & Reversibility
entries.hint: A thermodynamic process is reversible only if it can be run backward through the exact same sequence of intermediate states, restoring both the system and its surroundings to their original condition with no net change anywhere in the universe — an idealisation no real physical process ever fully achieves, since any real change generates at least some entropy. Equilibrium is the specific state a system settles into when left alone long enough that nothing further changes.
entries.note: Thomson, W. [Lord Kelvin] (1851). 'On the Dynamical Theory of Heat.' Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, 20, 261–288, at the University of Glasgow. Real engines and processes are always somewhat irreversible, generating entropy and wasting some potential useful work as a result; Carnot's maximum-efficiency limit (see st3) applies specifically and only to the idealised, unreachable reversible case.

entries.label: Damping & Resonance
entries.hint: Real oscillating systems lose energy over time to friction or other resistance — damping — causing their swings to gradually shrink unless continuously driven; drive such a system at exactly its own natural frequency, however, and even a small periodic push can build the oscillation's amplitude up dramatically, since each push arrives in step with the system's own motion. The interplay between how strongly a system is damped and how sharply it resonates determines everything from a car's suspension response to a radio tuner's selectivity.
entries.note: Strutt, J.W. [Lord Rayleigh] (1877). The Theory of Sound, Vol. I. London: Macmillan, largely written at Terling Place, Essex, and at Cambridge. Rayleigh's treatment gave engineers the first systematic mathematical vocabulary — natural frequency, damping ratio, quality factor — for analysing driven oscillating systems generally, well beyond the acoustic problems the book was nominally about.

entries.label: Viscosity
entries.hint: Viscosity measures a fluid's internal resistance to flowing — how much it resists being sheared into layers moving at different speeds — with honey and syrup sitting at the thick, high-viscosity end and air and water at the thin, low-viscosity end. Jean Léonard Marie Poiseuille's precise measurements of how liquids move through narrow tubes gave viscosity its first rigorous quantitative law, directly motivated by his medical interest in blood flow through capillaries.
entries.note: Poiseuille, J.L.M. (1840–46). 'Recherches expérimentales sur le mouvement des liquides dans les tubes de très petits diamètres.' Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, conducted in Paris, where Poiseuille trained and practised as a physician before turning to fluid mechanics research. The resulting Hagen–Poiseuille equation (co-derived independently by German engineer Gotthilf Hagen) remains standard for predicting flow rate through pipes, blood vessels, and narrow channels generally.

entries.label: Statistical Ensembles
entries.hint: Rather than tracking one single system's exact evolution, Josiah Willard Gibbs proposed imagining a vast hypothetical collection — an 'ensemble' — of identically prepared copies of the system, differing only in their microscopic details, and computing macroscopic properties as averages over the whole ensemble. Different ensembles (fixed energy, fixed temperature, fixed particle number and pressure) correspond to different realistic experimental conditions, and Gibbs showed they all agree in the limit of very large systems.
entries.note: Gibbs, J.W. (1902). Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics. New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, written at Yale University, where Gibbs held the first American professorship in mathematical physics. Gibbs's ensemble framework, formulated independently of and somewhat later than Boltzmann's and Maxwell's more physically motivated approaches, gave statistical mechanics its modern, fully general mathematical foundation, extending cleanly to quantum statistical mechanics in the following decades.
